meta.title: Swiss tables: control bytes, SIMD group probing, tombstones and 7/8 load
meta.subject: Computer science

story.title: How a byte per slot lets a hash table check 16 slots with one instruction

tldr: A Swiss table is an open-addressing hash table with a 1-byte tag per slot. One SIMD instruction compares a lookup key's 7-bit tag against 16 slots (8 in Go), so full key comparisons are rare. A probe stops at the first empty slot, deletes write a tombstone only when needed, and tables run up to 7/8 full.
why: Why it matters: hash maps sit on the hot path of most programs, and Rust's std map, Go's built-in map since 1.24 and Google's Abseil all use this layout.

cards.title: A strip of sticky notes lets the clerk check a whole row at a glance
cards.brief: A mailroom row has a strip of tiny fingerprints, one per pigeonhole. One glance shows which holes could hold your parcel, and a blank spot proves the parcel was never pushed to another row.

cards.title: Six ideas you need first
cards.brief: Hashing to an index, chaining vs open addressing, load factor, SIMD compare + movemask, tombstones, cache lines.

cards.title: Rust, Go and Google C++ all store maps this way
cards.brief: Abseil (2017) → Rust std via hashbrown (1.36, 2019) → Go built-in map (1.24, 2025). One byte of metadata per slot, 7/8 max load. Rust's README claims ~2× the old map (vendor figure).

cards.title: "A flat hash table with a 1-byte tag array" hides five things
cards.brief: 7-bit tags can lie; empty vs deleted decides when a probe stops; probing is per group; erase sometimes writes empty; and 7/8 load is affordable only because probes are cheap.

cards.title: Chaining chases pointers; linear probing compares every key
cards.brief: Chained tables pay a pointer and a likely cache miss per entry. Plain linear probing clusters and compares full keys. Swiss tables keep it flat and filter with a byte per slot: 1 byte instead of 8.

cards.title: A strip of tags above each row of slots
cards.brief: Glance at the strip, open only the maybes. It breaks where tags collide (1 in 128), hops are triangular, and the strip lives in separate memory.

cards.title: Find: one compare, then hop only while the group is full
cards.brief:
Compare the key's 7-bit tag to 8 or 16 control bytes at once, check the few candidates, stop at the first empty slot, otherwise hop +1, +2, +3 groups. Erase writes either empty or a tombstone.

Step-through of lookup, miss, insert and erase inside.

cards.title: Almost half of 16-slot groups are full at 7/8 load
cards.brief:
False tag matches cost occupied/128 per group. The naive αW model predicts 1.13 groups per miss at 7/8; my simulator measures 2.09, because 47.6% of groups hold no empty slot.

Load-factor explorer inside.

cards.title: Filter cheaply for 16 slots, verify expensively for one
cards.brief: Separate "which slots could match" (two SIMD instructions on one cache line) from "does this slot match" (full compare, about once per lookup). Each piece, removed, breaks correctness or speed.

cards.title: Same core, three different group widths and growth schemes
cards.brief: Abseil uses 16-wide groups, Go 8, hashbrown 16 on SIMD. All run at 7/8. Go splits growth into ≤1024-slot tables; Abseil and hashbrown rehash everything.

cards.title: Tombstones, resize spikes and hash flooding
cards.brief: Tombstones eat growth budget until a rehash; whole-table rehash is O(n); predictable hashes allow flooding. Ruby's Swiss-style layer regressed real benchmarks (+1.77% geomean).

cards.title: Go added a directory of tables; hashbrown added a scalar fallback
cards.brief: Abseil is the reference. Go 1.24 maps use a directory of ≤1024-slot tables and randomise iteration; Rust's std uses SipHash while the hashbrown crate defaults to foldhash.

cards.title: CPU design settled; work moved to GPUs, deletes and theory
cards.brief: DLHT (HPDC 2024), WarpSpeed (ALENEX 2026), a SIMD hash-table analysis (arXiv, Oct 2026), GPU tables. No peer-reviewed Swiss-table critique found.

cards.title: Tombstone-free deletes at SIMD speed are unsolved
cards.brief: Deletes without tombstones, bounded insert tails, hash speed versus attack resistance, and a rigorous probe model for real implementations.

cards.title: From open addressing to Go 1.24 in 70 years
cards.brief: Linear probing → hash-flooding attacks (2003) → SipHash (2012) → Swiss tables (2017) → Rust std (2019) → Go 1.24 (2025).

cards.title: Run a 1-second simulator and break the erase rule
cards.brief: swiss_sim.py reproduces every measured number in this dive. Make the tag 3 bits, or make erase always write empty, and watch what breaks.

cold.q: A Swiss table tags each slot with 7 bits of the key's hash. How often does a wrong occupied slot match your key's tag by chance?
cold.reveal: 1 in 128: 7 independent bits give 27 = 128 values. At 7/8 load a 16-wide group has ~14 occupied slots, so about 0.11 wasted key compares per group visit.

erase.q: Abseil erases a key from the table. Which marker does it write in the control byte?
options: Empty if the slot was never inside a full probe window, else a tombstone
erase.reveal: Empty only when no probe could have passed through, otherwise a tombstone. Always-empty would make present keys look absent; always-tombstone fills the table with dead slots (19 rehashes versus 7 in my churn test).

miss.q: Load 7/8, 16-slot groups. Naive math (each slot full with probability 7/8) says a missing key visits 1.13 groups. What does a simulator measure?
miss.reveal: About 2.09 groups (my simulator, aligned groups, deterministic seed). 47.6% of groups have no empty slot, not 11.8%, because keys land unevenly and overflow spills into neighbours.

w8.q: Halve the group width from 16 to 8 slots at 7/8 load. How many more groups does a missing-key lookup visit?
w8.reveal: About 1.4×: 2.93 versus 2.09 groups in the simulator. Narrower groups fill more often (60% versus 48%), but each hop is also cheaper, so width is a tradeoff, not a free win.

churn.q: Churn test: 80% load, 60,000 delete+insert rounds. Compared with always writing tombstones, how many rehashes does the "never full" erase rule need?
churn.reveal: About 2.7× fewer (7 versus 19). Fewer tombstones means the growth budget lasts longer. Single seed, simplified erase test.

questions.q: What exactly is compared in one SIMD step, and what comes out?
questions.a: The key's 7-bit tag is broadcast to every byte of a register and compared to the group's 16 (or 8) control bytes; the result is packed into a bitmask with one bit per slot. Set bits are candidate slots.

questions.q: Why does a probe stop at an empty slot but not at a deleted one?
questions.a: Inserts fill the earliest free slot on the probe path, so a key absent from every group up to the first empty cannot be further along. A deleted slot may have been full when some other key overflowed past it, so stopping there could hide that key.

questions.q: Walk the miss lookup of K2 in the trace.
questions.a: G1 has no matching tag and no empty slot, so hop +1 to G2; G2 has no match and an empty slot, so stop with "absent" after 2 groups.

questions.q: What happens on insert when growth_left is zero?
questions.a: The table rehashes first: a same-size rehash that clears tombstones if enough are present, otherwise growth to 2·capacity+1, then the insert proceeds.
The top bit of the control byte marks empty/deleted/sentinel, which makes "full", "empty or deleted" and "empty" single cheap tests. That leaves 7 bits for the fingerprint.

questions.q: Why is the load factor 7/8 and not 1/2?
questions.a: Because a probe step is one cheap group compare, not a slot-by-slot walk with full key compares. Memory per entry drops and the simulator shows hits still cost about 1.1 groups at 7/8.

questions.q: Why triangular steps over groups instead of +1 each time?
questions.a: Linear steps make full groups clump, so one overloaded neighbourhood lengthens every probe crossing it. Triangular offsets scatter retries, and with a power-of-two group count still visit every group exactly once.

questions.q: Why does the naive α^W model underestimate probes?
questions.a: Keys do not land in groups evenly: occupancy is roughly Poisson with mean αW, so many groups overflow and spill into later ones. At 7/8 with W=16 about 47.6% of groups are full, not 11.8%.

questions.q: What if erase always wrote empty?
questions.a: Present keys that once overflowed past the erased slot would be reported absent. The simulator's test 2 in the hands-on shows it.

questions.q: What if the table never rehashed in place and only doubled?
questions.a: Tombstone-heavy tables would double needlessly, wasting memory. Same-size rehash exists to reclaim tombstone budget.
Fewer hops at high load but a larger window (still ~one cache line with AVX2, not on SSE2), more occupied slots per group means more false matches per visit, and portability suffers.

questions.q: How would you degrade a Swiss table you can feed keys to?
questions.a: Find keys whose hashes land in the same groups: with a known or leaked seed, every key probes the same long path (HashDoS). Use a keyed hash like SipHash.

questions.q: Why is a random seed alone not enough?
questions.a: Aumasson, Bernstein and Boßlet (2012) showed weak hash functions can leak the seed (e.g. via collision behaviour or iteration order), so the hash must be a keyed PRF-like function such as SipHash.

questions.q: How would you stress the "never full" erase rule?
questions.a: Churn near the load ceiling so windows alternate between full and non-full: erases flip between tombstone and empty and rehashes get timed near the boundary.

questions.q: How does Go's directory of tables relate to extendible hashing?
questions.a: The directory is indexed by the high hash bits, each table has a local depth, entries can point to the same table, and a full table splits and doubles the directory only when its local depth equals the global depth.

questions.q: How does DLHT answer the tombstone problem?
questions.a: It uses closed addressing with cache-line chaining so a deleted slot is reusable immediately, at the price of chaining instead of open addressing.

questions.q: Is there a tombstone-free delete for SIMD open addressing that is as fast as erase-to-tombstone?
questions.a: Unsettled; the never-full trick avoids most but not all, and chained or concurrent designs trade lookup shape for it.

questions.q: When is a Swiss table slower than the structure it replaced?
questions.a: Ruby's st_table experiment lost on real benchmarks; tiny maps and unpredictable-key small maps (Go #70700) were weak spots until fixed. The answer depends on workload and hash.
